analysis.one_liner: Excludes productivity and sales bonuses from overtime pay calculations.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have excluded bonuses and commissions from the overtime pay rate, died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal overtime law says most workers must earn time-and-a-half on their "regular rate" of pay, and that rate currently includes most bonuses and commissions — so when a worker earns a performance bonus, the employer has to pay a slightly higher overtime rate too. This bill would have written those bonuses out of the regular rate, as long as they came from a written gainsharing, incentive, commission, or performance-bonus plan [S2][S3]. The practical effect is that employers would owe less overtime pay to workers who earn bonuses. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with bonus, commission, or incentive pay plans — especially in sales-heavy and manufacturing workplaces — would save money on every overtime hour worked by a bonus-earning employee, because overtime would no longer be recalculated to include the bonus [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers with bonus and commission plans

how_it_helps.text: Excludes payments from written gainsharing, incentive bonus, commission, or performance-contingent bonus plans from the "regular rate" used to compute overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S2][S3].
Requires that such plans be in writing, available to employees, and based on a stated formula, so the exclusion is not automatic for informal bonuses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who earn productivity or sales bonuses would receive a lower overtime rate, since the bonus would no longer be counted in the pay the overtime multiplier is applied to [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Workers' overtime pay would shrink: under current law a bonus raises the regular rate, so each overtime hour pays more; this bill would remove that boost for plan-based bonuses [S2][S3].

The bill would remove an existing compliance burden that requires employers to retroactively recompute overtime whenever bonuses are paid, which is the change employers would welcome and workers would not [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a straightforward cost saving to employers by reducing what bonus-earning workers receive for overtime hours. The written-plan and formula requirements keep the exclusion from covering truly discretionary payments, but the core effect is to shift money from workers' overtime paychecks to employers' labor budgets. It died without a single cosponsor, so it never had the support to become law anyway.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action until the two-year Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Introduced January 28, 2021, with no cosponsors ever added [S4][S5].
Referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction; that referral is the last action in its history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers, in the sense that the current overtime rule — which counts most bonuses in the overtime rate — stayed intact. Employers who would have saved on overtime gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers kept the overtime rule as-is

for.name: Rep. Ken Calvert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract a single cosponsor [S4][S5].

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Only one Republican sponsored the bill, no cosponsors of either party signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers with bonus, commission, or incentive pay plans
industries.note: The bill would have reduced employers' overtime costs by excluding plan-based bonuses from the regular overtime rate, meaning workers who earn bonuses would get less for each overtime hour worked. Employers' gain is directly the workers' lost overtime pay [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Sales-heavy and manufacturing workplaces (retail, distribution, piece-rate production)
industries.note: These are the industries where gainsharing, commission, and productivity bonus plans are most common, so they would benefit most from not having to recompute overtime when bonuses are paid.
